text: Transfer learning typically updates every parameter of a pretrained backbone. We propose freezing the backbone and learning small low-rank adapter matrices instead, updating less than one percent of all weights during adaptation.
Each frozen weight matrix receives an update expressed as the product of two low-rank factors. Only the factors are optimized while the original weights stay fixed throughout training.
The rank of the factors controls capacity: rank 8 suffices for classification tasks while rank 16 helps generation. A scaling factor on the adapter output stabilizes training at startup.
On ImageNet transfer the proposed approach reduces training cost by 40 percent compared to full fine-tuning, measured in total GPU hours across three seeds.
GLUE evaluation reaches an average score of 89.2, within 0.4 points of the full fine-tuning baseline while training one tenth of the parameters.
Ablating the adapter placement shows that attention projections matter more than feed-forward layers across all tested model depths.
Full fine-tuning updates all parameters and remains the default in most libraries despite its computational cost and memory footprint.
Prompt tuning compresses task instructions into a sequence of soft prompts, but its capacity is limited for knowledge-heavy adaptation tasks.
Training curves converge within three epochs, and the optimizer state for the adapters occupies 340 MB on a single consumer GPU.
Cross-device federated learning must protect each participant contribution. We aggregate clipped client updates under calibrated Gaussian noise with formal differential privacy guarantees.
Each client update is clipped to a bounded norm before aggregation, limiting the influence any single participant can exert on the shared model.
The noise multiplier is calibrated to a privacy budget with epsilon 8 for the reported runs, and delta fixed at one over the client population.
On CIFAR-10 the proposed scheme keeps accuracy within 1.5 points of the non-private baseline at the same privacy budget.
The proposed scheme reduces communication rounds by half through server-side momentum correction during aggregation.
Heterogeneous clients with skewed label distributions degrade accuracy by at most 2 points under identical noise calibration.
Centralised training on pooled data updates all parameters and cannot satisfy privacy regulations for sensitive user corpora.
Secure aggregation hides individual updates cryptographically but leaks information across repeated rounds, unlike formal guarantees.
An adaptive clipping schedule decays the norm bound over rounds, trading utility for a tighter privacy accounting profile.
